question:
A 42-year-old man comes to the physician because of severe epigastric pain for a week. The pain is constant and he describes it as 6 out of 10 in intensity. The pain radiates to his back and is worse after meals. He has had several episodes of nausea and vomiting during this period. He has taken ibuprofen for multiple similar episodes of pain during the past 6 months. He also has had a 5.4-kg (12-lb) weight loss over the past 4 months. He has a 12-year history of drinking 3 to 4 pints of rum daily. He has been hospitalized three times for severe abdominal pain in the past 3 years. He appears ill. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 87/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. There is severe epigastric tenderness to palpation. Bowel sounds are normal. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL
Leukocyte count 7,800/mm3
Serum
Glucose 106 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL
Amylase 150 U/L
A CT of the abdomen is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management for this patient?"?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Chronic alcohol consumption -> chronic pancreatitis -> severe epigastric pain -> nausea and vomiting -> weight loss -> history of hospitalizations for abdominal pain -> ill-appearance -> epigastric tenderness -> laboratory studies showing elevated amylase -> possible pancreatic insufficiency -> need for long-term management -> Pancreatic enzyme therapy -> 80%
enhanced_information: The patient's presentation with chronic alcohol consumption, severe epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, elevated amylase, and possible pancreatic insufficiency suggests chronic pancreatitis. Long-term management should involve pancreatic enzyme therapy to address pancreatic insufficiency. The evidence paths support the relationship between chronic pancreatitis and epigastric pain, as well as the connection between chronic pancreatitis and symptoms like nausea and vomiting.
analysis: The patient's presentation with chronic alcohol consumption, severe epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, elevated amylase, and possible pancreatic insufficiency strongly suggests chronic pancreatitis. Long-term management of chronic pancreatitis involves addressing pancreatic insufficiency, which can be effectively managed with pancreatic enzyme therapy.
